description: A collection of YC interview questions with the user's prepared answers, one item per question (#65, #69). Queries are the questions as an interviewer would phrase them in the moment, so they rarely share words with the stored question.

documents.title: What are you working on?
documents.text: Q: What are you working on? A: Larderly tells independent restaurants what every dish really costs. You photograph supplier invoices and we turn them into live plate costs and price alerts.

documents.title: Why did you pick this idea?
documents.text: Q: Why did you pick this idea? A: I spent six years doing the books for my family's restaurant. Every April the accountant told us we had lost money on dishes we thought were our best sellers.

documents.title: How do you know people need this?
documents.text: Q: How do you know people need what you're making? A: 38 restaurants pay us, most found us through another owner, and the ones who activate keep scanning invoices every week without being reminded.

documents.title: Why now?
documents.text: Q: Why now? A: Food costs rose about 25% in three years, phone cameras and on-device text recognition got good enough to read crumpled invoices, and POS systems finally opened their APIs.

documents.title: Who are your competitors?
documents.text: Q: Who are your competitors? A: The incumbents sell to multi-location groups with long onboarding. For a single restaurant the competitor is a spreadsheet, a shoebox of invoices, or nothing.

documents.title: What do you understand that others don't?
documents.text: Q: What do you understand about your business that other companies in it just don't get? A: Nobody in a small kitchen will count inventory every week, but they already handle every invoice. Starting from invoices instead of counts is why we get adoption.

documents.title: How do you make money?
documents.text: Q: How do you or will you make money? A: Subscriptions: $29 per location for Basic and $149 for Pro. Later, a small fee on purchasing once restaurants reorder through us.

documents.title: How big could this be?
documents.text: Q: How big can this get? A: About 390,000 independent US restaurants at $1,800 a year is a $700M subscription market before payments on purchasing, which is many times larger.

documents.title: What's your growth rate?
documents.text: Q: How fast are you growing? A: Revenue has grown 22% month over month for the last three months, from $9,800 to $14,200 MRR.

documents.title: How did you meet your co-founder?
documents.text: Q: How long have the founders known each other and how did you meet? A: Priya and I met in 2019 volunteering at a community kitchen in Oakland. We built a donation tracker together there before we ever talked about a company.

documents.title: Who writes the code?
documents.text: Q: Who writes code, or does other technical work on your product? A: Priya built the backend and the invoice pipeline, Tomás owns the iOS app, and I write the integration scripts and SQL reports. Nothing is outsourced.

documents.title: What's the hardest technical problem?
documents.text: Q: What is the hardest technical problem you've solved? A: Mapping messy invoice lines like 'CHKN THGH BNLS 40#' to a canonical ingredient and unit, across hundreds of suppliers that each abbreviate differently.

documents.title: How do you get customers?
documents.text: Q: How will you get users? A: Walking into restaurants mid-afternoon and from owner referrals. Each restaurant introduces us to about 0.6 other restaurants, and we give a free month for each referral.

documents.title: What's the biggest risk?
documents.text: Q: What's the biggest thing that could kill you? A: Restaurant closures. We screen for restaurants open more than two years and expand within groups, where churn is much lower.

documents.title: Why will you win?
documents.text: Q: Why are you the right team? A: I lived this problem in a kitchen for six years and Priya built financial systems that handled millions of transactions a day. We already have the customers' trust.

documents.title: What would you do with the money?
documents.text: Q: What will you do with the money? A: Hire a customer success lead from the restaurant world and a second iOS engineer, launch Android, and get to 300 restaurants.

documents.title: What surprised you most?
documents.text: Q: What's the most surprising thing you've learned from users? A: Owners care less about the dashboard than the text message. The daily 'your avocado price went up 14%' alert drives most of our retention.

documents.title: Who is your ideal user?
documents.text: Q: Who exactly is your customer? A: An owner-operator with one to five locations and no finance staff, usually doing the books themselves late at night after service.

documents.title: How long have you been working on it?
documents.text: Q: How long have you been working on this, and full time? A: Since March 2025, both founders full time since day one.

documents.title: What's your churn?
documents.text: Q: Are people leaving? A: Two restaurants left in six months, both for reasons outside the product: one closed and one was acquired. Net revenue retention is 128%.

documents.title: Why isn't someone bigger doing this?
documents.text: Q: Why hasn't a big company already done this? A: The money in restaurant software has been in large groups, so incumbents built for finance teams. Small restaurants looked too cheap to sell to, until you can sell with a phone and no onboarding.

documents.title: What have you learned from talking to users?
documents.text: Q: What did you learn from your first users? A: Our first version asked for weekly inventory counts and nobody did them. Switching to invoices doubled activation in a month.

documents.title: Who would you hire next?
documents.text: Q: If you could hire one person tomorrow, who would it be? A: Someone who has run a restaurant floor and loves software, to do onboarding and customer success.

documents.title: What's your unfair advantage?
documents.text: Q: What's your unfair advantage? A: A labelled set of 2,000 real invoices and a daily price feed from a produce co-op, which nobody targeting small restaurants has.

documents.title: What's your gross margin?
documents.text: Q: What are your unit economics? A: Gross margin is about 81%, customers come mostly through referrals, and a Pro customer pays back their acquisition cost in under two months.

documents.title: How do you decide what to build?
documents.text: Q: How do you decide what to work on? A: Every feature has to come from at least three restaurants asking for it, and we test it with the five pilot restaurants before anyone else sees it.

documents.title: Have you raised money?
documents.text: Q: Have you raised money before? A: Yes, a $750,000 pre-seed on an $8M post-money SAFE, led by Northgate Ventures, in September 2025.

documents.title: What's your burn?
documents.text: Q: How much money do you spend per month and how long will it last? A: About $31,000 a month, with roughly 13 months of runway.

documents.title: What's an example of a user's success?
documents.text: Q: Tell me about a user who loves you. A: Casa Verde found their carnitas plate had gone from 28% to 36% food cost and recovered about $2,100 a month by repricing.

documents.title: What's a disagreement you had?
documents.text: Q: Tell me about a time you and your co-founder disagreed. A: Priya wanted to build Android before Pro; I wanted Pro first. We ran the numbers on what customers asked for, shipped Pro, and it tripled revenue per restaurant.

documents.title: What's the long-term vision?
documents.text: Q: Where will this be in ten years? A: The operating system for independent restaurants' money: costs, purchasing, payments to suppliers and eventually working capital.

documents.title: Why should an independent restaurant trust you?
documents.text: Q: Why would a restaurant trust a startup with its books? A: We delete invoice images after 90 days, they can export everything any time, and we answer support texts in about six minutes.

documents.title: What would make you quit?
documents.text: Q: What would make you give up on this? A: If restaurants that see their real food costs still don't change prices or suppliers. So far 70% change something within a month.

documents.title: What is your activation rate?
documents.text: Q: What fraction of signups actually use it? A: About 55% of trials activate, meaning ten invoices scanned and five recipes costed, and 78% of activated restaurants pay.

documents.title: What's something you got wrong?
documents.text: Q: What's the biggest mistake you've made so far? A: We spent $3,200 on ads in the spring. Every trial cost $640 and none converted, because owners trust other owners, not ads.

documents.title: What's your pricing based on?
documents.text: Q: How did you set your price? A: Pro saves a typical restaurant at least ten times its price in food cost. We tested $99 flat against tiered pricing and tiers won on revenue without hurting conversion.

documents.title: Are you open to pivoting?
documents.text: Q: Would you change the idea if we asked? A: We'd change the product in a heartbeat, but not the customer: independent restaurants are who we want to serve.

documents.title: How technical are the founders?
documents.text: Q: Are you technical? A: Priya is deeply technical, ten years of backend and payments. I'm technical enough to write SQL and Python and ship the integrations.

documents.title: Where do you see yourselves after YC?
documents.text: Q: What do you want to have achieved by demo day? A: 100 paying restaurants, $40,000 MRR, and Clover live so we cover the three biggest POS systems in our segment.

documents.title: What's a metric you watch daily?
documents.text: Q: What metric do you look at every day? A: Invoices scanned per active restaurant. If it drops below three a week, that restaurant is about to churn and we call them.

documents.title: What else have you built?
documents.text: Q: What's the most impressive thing you've built or achieved? A: I turned my family's restaurant from losing money to an 8% margin in two years, mostly by fixing purchasing.

documents.title: How does the product work technically?
documents.text: Q: Walk me through how it works under the hood. A: The phone finds the invoice, reads it on device, a server model maps lines to ingredients, and we join that with recipes and POS sales to get cost per plate.

documents.title: What's your distribution advantage?
documents.text: Q: Is there a channel you have that others don't? A: Bay Produce Co-op lets us present at their monthly member meetings, which put us in front of about 200 independent owners.

documents.title: Anything else we should know?
documents.text: Q: Is there anything else you'd like to tell us? A: Every one of our first ten customers still pays us, and three of them have offered to talk to you.

documents.title: What are your weekly goals?
documents.text: Q: What's your goal for this week? A: Sign four new restaurants, finish the Clover integration spec, and get the weekly margin text into the hands of the pilot group.
